text: The Panavia Tornado is a family of twin-engine, variable-sweep wing multi-role combat aircraft jointly developed and manufactured by Italy, the United Kingdom, and Germany. It consists of three primary variants: the Tornado IDS (interdictor/strike) fighter-bomber, the Tornado ECR (electronic combat/reconnaissance) SEAD aircraft, and the Tornado ADV (air defence variant) interceptor. Developed by Panavia Aircraft GmbH, a tri-national consortium comprising British Aerospace (formerly British Aircraft Corporation), MBB of West Germany, and Aeritalia of Italy, the Tornado first flew on 14 August 1974 and entered service between 1979 and 1980. Due to its multirole capabilities, it replaced several different aircraft types in the air forces of its operators. The Royal Saudi Air Force (RSAF) is the only export operator of the Tornado, in addition to the three original partner nations. A training and evaluation unit, the Tri-National Tornado Training Establishment (TTTE), operated from RAF Cottesmore and maintained international cooperation beyond production. The Tornado is the only non-American-developed aircraft currently approved to carry United States nuclear weapons under NATO's Nuclear Planning Group. The Tornado was operated by the Royal Air Force (RAF), Italian Air Force, and RSAF during the Gulf War of 1991, conducting numerous low-altitude penetrating strike missions. It was also used in the Bosnian War, Kosovo War, Iraq War, the 2011 Libyan civil war, and in smaller roles in Afghanistan, Yemen, and Syria. Including all variants, 990 aircraft were built. The concept of variable-geometry wings was explored in the 1960s to combine the maneuverability of straight wings with the speed of swept wings. The UK cancelled the BAC TSR-2 and the US F-111K in 1965 and 1967, respectively, and sought a replacement for the Avro Vulcan and Blackburn Buccaneer. Britain and France initiated the BAC/Dassault AFVG project in 1965, which ended with French withdrawal in 1967. West Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, and Canada formed a working group in 1968 to replace the Lockheed F-104G Starfighter, initially called the Multi Role Aircraft (MRA) and later renamed the Multi Role Combat Aircraft (MRCA). Due to diverse requirements, a single multirole aircraft was developed. Britain joined in 1968, and a memorandum of agreement was signed between the UK, West Germany, and Italy in May 1969. By the end of 1968, the six countries planned to purchase 1,500 aircraft. Canada and Belgium withdrew before long-term commitments; Canada found the project politically unpalatable, and France offered Belgium the Dassault Mirage 5. On 26 March 1969, the UK, Germany, Italy, and the Netherlands agreed to form Panavia Aircraft GmbH to develop and manufacture the MRCA. The project aimed to produce an aircraft capable of tactical strike, reconnaissance, air defence, and maritime missions. Various design concepts, including fixed-wing and single-engine options, were studied. The Netherlands withdrew in 1970, citing complexity, and Germany reduced its order from 600 to 324 in 1972. It is suggested Germany initially placed a high order to secure design influence in Germany. The UK and West Germany each held a 42.5% share of the workload, with Italy holding 15%, influenced by political negotiations. The front fuselage and tail were assigned to BAC (now BAE Systems), the centre fuselage to MBB (now part of Airbus), and the wings to Aeritalia (now Leonardo). A separate company, Turbo-Union, formed in June 1970, developed the RB199 engines with ownership split 40% Rolls-Royce, 40% MTU, and 20% FIAT. In May 1970, two designs were selected: the single-seat Panavia 100 and the twin-seat Panavia 200, with the latter preferred by the RAF. The aircraft was briefly called the Panavia Panther. In September 1971, the three governments signed an Intention to Proceed (ITP) document, designating the aircraft for low-level strike missions, with the UK's Chief of the Defence Staff stating that two-thirds of the front-line fighting force would consist of this aircraft. The first of fifteen development aircraft, including nine prototypes (P01 to P09) and six pre-series (PS11 to PS16), flew on 14 August 1974 at Manching, Germany. Pilot Paul Millett described the flight as smooth and almost simulated. Flight testing required modifications, including re-profiling engine intakes and fuselage to reduce surging and buffeting at supersonic speeds. Jim Quinn, a developer of the Tornado simulation software and engine controls, noted that the prototype could reach supercruise safely, but engines had safety issues at high altitude during deceleration due to combustion pressure backfiring; engine controls automatically increased idle settings with altitude, leading to one aircraft being stuck at Mach 1.2 and unable to decelerate. A nose-wheel steering augmentation system was needed to counteract destabilization during landing with the thrust reverser deployed. Two prototypes were lost due to pilot error in ground collisions, and a third was seriously damaged by pilot-induced pitch oscillation. Designers incorporated advanced stability augmentation systems and autopilots, similar to those in the F-16. Failure testing of the triplex analogue CSAS was conducted on flight control rigs, complicated by variable-sweep wings and heavy payloads. The contract for Batch 1 aircraft was signed on 29 July 1976. The first production aircraft flew on 10 July 1979 at BAe Warton, with the first deliveries to the RAF and German Air Force on 5 and 6 June 1979, respectively. The first Italian Tornado was delivered on 25 September 1981. The TTTE officially opened on 29 January 1981 and remained active until 31 March 1999. The 500th Tornado was delivered to West Germany on 19 December 1987. Saudi Arabia was the only export customer, as part of the Al-Yamamah arms deal between British Aerospace and the Saudi government. Oman committed to purchasing eight Tornado F2s and associated equipment for £250 million in August 1985 but cancelled the order in 1990 due to financial difficulties. Australia considered joining the MRCA programme to replace its Dassault Mirage IIIs and ultimately selected the F/A-18 Hornet. Canada also chose the F/A-18 after considering the Tornado. Japan considered the Tornado in the 1980s, along with the F-16 and F/A-18, before selecting the Mitsubishi F-2. In the 1990s, Taiwan and South Korea expressed interest in acquiring small numbers of Tornado ECR aircraft. In 2001, EADS proposed a Tornado ECR variant with enhanced electronic warfare capabilities for Australia. Production ended in 1998, with the final batch going to the RSAF, which ordered 96 IDS Tornados. In June 2011, the Tornado fleet collectively flew over one million flying hours. Aviation author Jon Lake noted that the Panavia consortium produced just under 1,000 Tornados, making it one of the most successful postwar bomber programs. In 2008, AirForces Monthly called the Tornado "for more than a quarter of a century... the most important military aircraft in Western Europe." The Tornado is designed as a low-level penetration aircraft with variable-sweep wings enabling efficient high-speed and low-speed flight. Its mission during the Cold War involved delivering conventional and nuclear weapons against Warsaw Pact forces in Eastern Europe. The variable wing geometry minimizes drag during low-level flight. Advanced navigation and flight computers, including a fly-by-wire system, reduce pilot workload. For long-range missions, it has a retractable refuelling probe. As a multirole aircraft, it replaced multiple specialized aircraft types with a single platform, either through standard Tornados or modified variants like the Tornado ECR. The most extensive modification was the Tornado ADV, which was stretched and armed with long-range anti-aircraft missiles for interception. Operators have conducted life extension and upgrade programs, projecting continued service until 2025. To perform as a low-level supersonic strike aircraft, the Tornado required good high- and low-speed flight characteristics. A swept or delta wing is efficient at high speed but inefficient at low speed; the variable-sweep wing enables performance at both speeds. The wing sweep angle ranges from 25 to 67 degrees, with each angle having a specific speed range. Some Tornado ADVs had an automatic wing-sweep system. When wings are swept back, drag is reduced, aiding high-speed low-level flight. Weapons pylons pivot with the wing sweep so stores point in the direction of flight. Significant attention was given to short-field take-off and landing (STOL) performance, particularly in Germany. The Tornado can sweep wings to 25 degrees, deploy full-span flaps and leading edge slats, and use thrust reversers for excellent low-speed handling. The aircraft has a tandem-seat cockpit with a pilot and navigator/weapons officer, using electromechanical and electro-optical controls. Dials and switches are mounted on either side of a centrally placed CRT monitor for navigation, communications, and weapons control. BAE Systems developed the Tornado Advanced Radar Display Information System (TARDIS), a 32.5-centimetre multi-function display, replacing the rear cockpit's Combined Radar and Projected Map Display; the RAF began installing it on the GR4 fleet in 2004. The primary flight controls are a fly-by-wire hybrid, consisting of an analogue quadruplex Command and Stability Augmentation System (CSAS) connected to a digital Autopilot & Flight Director System (AFDS), with mechanical reversion retained for safety. Artificial feel is built into the controls, adjusting automatically to wing profile and flight attitude changes. The flight stability system compensates for changes in flight dynamics due to a wide range of munitions. The Tornado has a combined navigation/attack Doppler radar that scans for targets and conducts fully automated terrain-following for all-weather, hands-off low-level flight. The Tornado ADV uses the AI.24 Foxhunter radar, capable of tracking up to 20 targets at ranges up to 160 kilometres (100 miles). The Tornado was one of the first aircraft to feature a digital data bus, with Link 16 JTIDS integration on the F3 variant enabling data exchange with friendly aircraft. The Tornado ECR, operated by Germany and Italy, is dedicated to Suppression of Enemy Air Defences (SEAD) and is equipped with an emitter-locator system (ELS) to detect radar use. German ECRs have a Honeywell infrared imaging system for reconnaissance. RAF and RSAF Tornados have the Laser Range Finder and Marked Target Seekers (LRMTS) for targeting laser-guided munitions. In 1991, the RAF introduced the Thermal Imaging and Laser Designator (TIALD) system.
